meta.title: Irish Elections
sources: Wikipedia: Irish general and presidential election articles 1922–2025

presEras.label: The office nobody contested
presEras.blurb: Ireland's presidency is largely ceremonial, and for most of its history the parties agreed a candidate rather than fight for it. Five of the thirteen elections here were never actually held: a single nominee was returned unopposed, in 1952, 1974, 1976, 1983 and again in 2004. The contests that did happen were Fianna Fáil's to lose, and it lost only once.

presEras.label: Mary Robinson onwards
presEras.blurb: In 1990 Mary Robinson trailed Brian Lenihan on first preferences and won on transfers, the first non-Fianna Fáil president and the first woman, and the office has been contested and consequential since. Michael D. Higgins served two terms; Catherine Connolly's 63% in 2025 is the highest first-preference share the presidency has recorded.

legEras.label: The Free State
legEras.blurb: The first Dáil elections were fought over the Treaty by the two halves of Sinn Féin, and the losers of the civil war abstained from the parliament they had lost in. Cumann na nGaedheal governed a decade of austerity and state-building, and in 1932 handed power to the men it had recently been shooting at, which is the single most important thing that happened in Irish democracy.

legEras.label: De Valera's Ireland
legEras.blurb: Fianna Fáil in power for all but six of twenty-five years, a new constitution in 1937, neutrality through the Emergency, and two inter-party governments assembled from everyone else when the electorate tired of it. The republic was declared in 1949 by a coalition led by a party that had opposed it.

legEras.label: Lemass to the crash of 1977
legEras.blurb: The economy opened, the Fianna Fáil vote held, and the Fine Gael and Labour parties learned to run as a National Coalition. The 1977 election was won by Fianna Fáil on a manifesto of abolished rates and car tax, a landslide that produced a fiscal crisis and, within two years, Charles Haughey.

legEras.label: Three elections in eighteen months
legEras.blurb: The instability of the early 1980s gave way to Haughey and Reynolds, then to a rainbow coalition assembled without an election, then to Bertie Ahern's three consecutive wins on the back of the Celtic Tiger. Turnout fell throughout.

legEras.label: After the crash
legEras.blurb: In 2011 Fianna Fáil lost fifty-eight seats, the heaviest defeat any Irish governing party has suffered, and the duopoly that had defined the state since 1932 began to dissolve. By 2020 Sinn Féin topped the poll; by 2024 the old civil war parties governed together, which would have been unthinkable in any previous era on this page.
